title: Kabalagala
author: Maama Nakato
desc: Ripe sweet bananas mashed with cassava flour into a soft non-sticky dough, cut into rounds with a glass and shallow-fried — chewy, mildly sweet, and traditionally with no sugar in it at all.
longDesc: Kabalagala are the small banana pancakes sold everywhere in Uganda, and the traditional version is nothing but ripe sweet bananas and plain cassava flour — which gives a well-textured, mildly sweet, chewy pancake. This version adds two tablespoons of sugar and half a teaspoon of baking soda to soften it, and the cook who wrote it says twice, unprompted, that neither belongs traditionally. Leave both out and you have the older pancake; the recipe works either way.
ingredients: 720 to 960 ml (3 to 4 cups) cassava flour, sifted
2.5 ml (1/2 tsp) baking soda — not traditional
720 ml (3 cups) oil, for frying, or red palm oil
equipment: Cling film or clean plastic sheet
Round cookie cutter or a drinking glass
steps: Peel the ripe bananas, put them in a bowl and mash them until almost smooth.
Add the sugar and baking soda and mix well, if you are using them.
Add the cassava flour gradually until a soft non-sticky dough forms.
Lay a clean sheet of cling film on a flat surface and spread the dough out by hand to about a centimetre thick.
Cut out rounds with a cookie cutter or the rim of a glass, and repeat until the dough is used up.
Heat the oil over medium heat.
Fry the pancakes until golden brown and fragrant.
chefTips: Traditional kabalagala have no sugar and no baking soda. They are added here to soften the texture, and the cook who published this recipe says so herself, twice. Leave both out for the older pancake — plain cassava flour and ripe sweet banana gives a chewier, mildly sweet result.
Not all four cups of flour will be used. The cue is the dough not sticking to your hands or the bowl, and that is the only measure that matters.
Add the flour gradually. Dumped in at once you overshoot and get a stiff, dry dough you cannot rescue.
A centimetre thick, and spread by hand on cling film rather than rolled. The dough is too soft for a rolling pin.
Red palm oil is a legitimate and very good alternative for frying, and it changes the colour and flavour noticeably.
Medium heat. Too hot and they brown before the inside cooks.
Regular ripe bananas work in place of the small sweet ones, if that is what you have.
The ebook version of this recipe fries on high heat rather than medium and uses 3 to 4 cups of flour rather than 4 — a small unreconciled difference in the same cook's two publications.
commonMistakes: Adding all the flour at once.
Trying to roll the dough with a pin.
sources: Adapted from Sophia Musoki, 'How to Make Ugandan Banana Pancakes (Kabalagala)', A Kitchen In Uganda (4 August 2016), stated yield 10–12 pancakes — all quantities and the method are hers.

Her traditional-versus-hers flag is quoted closely because it matters: traditionally kabalagala are a mix of just plain cassava flour and ripe sweet bananas, and the sugar and baking soda are her additions to soften the texture. She states this twice in the same post.

Her notes that not all the flour will be used, that the non-sticky dough is the cue, and that kabalagala can also be fried in red palm oil are from the same post; the high-heat and 3-to-4-cup variation is from her ebook version (pp.32–33).
storage: 2 days in an airtight container at room temperature.
reheating: A minute in a dry pan. They go chewier, which is not a bad thing.
healthBenefits: Ripe bananas supply potassium and vitamin B6, and most of the sweetness comes from the fruit.
No dairy, no egg and, in the traditional version, no added sugar at all.
They are shallow-fried, so the oil is the limiting factor.
culturalNote: Kabalagala are sold from baskets and roadside tables all over Uganda and are among the first things a Ugandan child learns to want. The sugar-and-soda question is a real generational marker: the older pancake is chewier and much less sweet, and plenty of people prefer it.
